claim: TRAF2 is a component of TNF superfamily signalling complexes.
source: TRAF2 is a component of TNF superfamily signalling complexes and plays an essential role in the regulation and homeostasis of immune cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about TRAF2.

claim: TRAF2 plays an essential role in the regulation and homeostasis of immune cells.
source: TRAF2 is a component of TNF superfamily signalling complexes and plays an essential role in the regulation and homeostasis of immune cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about TRAF2.

claim: TRAF2 deficient mice die around birth.
source: TRAF2 deficient mice die around birth, therefore its role in adult tissues is not well-explored.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The role of TRAF2 in adult tissues is not well-explored.
source: TRAF2 deficient mice die around birth, therefore its role in adult tissues is not well-explored.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a gap in knowledge.

claim: The role of the TRAF2 RING is controversial.
source: Furthermore, the role of the TRAF2 RING is controversial.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a point of scientific debate.

claim: It has been claimed that the atypical TRAF2 RING cannot function as a ubiquitin E3 ligase.
source: It has been claimed that the atypical TRAF2 RING cannot function as a ubiquitin E3 ligase but counterclaimed that TRAF2 RING requires a co-factor, sphingosine-1-phosphate, that is generated by the enzyme sphingosine kinase 1, to function as an E3 ligase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a claim from the literature.

claim: It has been counterclaimed that TRAF2 RING requires a co-factor, sphingosine-1-phosphate, that is generated by the enzyme sphingosine kinase 1, to function as an E3 ligase.
source: It has been claimed that the atypical TRAF2 RING cannot function as a ubiquitin E3 ligase but counterclaimed that TRAF2 RING requires a co-factor, sphingosine-1-phosphate, that is generated by the enzyme sphingosine kinase 1, to function as an E3 ligase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a counterclaim from the literature.

claim: Keratinocyte-specific deletion of Traf2 disrupted TNF mediated NF-κB and MAP kinase signalling.
source: Keratinocyte-specific deletion of Traf2, but not Sphk1 deficiency, disrupted TNF mediated NF-κB and MAP kinase signalling and caused epidermal hyperplasia and psoriatic skin inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results.

claim: Sphk1 deficiency did not disrupt TNF mediated NF-κB and MAP kinase signalling in keratinocytes.
source: Keratinocyte-specific deletion of Traf2, but not Sphk1 deficiency, disrupted TNF mediated NF-κB and MAP kinase signalling and caused epidermal hyperplasia and psoriatic skin inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results.

claim: Keratinocyte-specific deletion of Traf2 caused epidermal hyperplasia and psoriatic skin inflammation.
source: Keratinocyte-specific deletion of Traf2, but not Sphk1 deficiency, disrupted TNF mediated NF-κB and MAP kinase signalling and caused epidermal hyperplasia and psoriatic skin inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and images in the results.

claim: The inflammation caused by keratinocyte-specific deletion of Traf2 was driven by TNF.
source: This inflammation was driven by TNF, cell death, non-canonical NF-κB and the adaptive immune system, and might therefore represent a clinically relevant model of psoriasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genetic experiments showing TNF deletion delays inflammation.

claim: The inflammation caused by keratinocyte-specific deletion of Traf2 was driven by cell death.
source: This inflammation was driven by TNF, cell death, non-canonical NF-κB and the adaptive immune system, and might therefore represent a clinically relevant model of psoriasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing apoptotic cells and rescue by caspase-8 deletion.

claim: The inflammation caused by keratinocyte-specific deletion of Traf2 was driven by non-canonical NF-κB.
source: This inflammation was driven by TNF, cell death, non-canonical NF-κB and the adaptive immune system, and might therefore represent a clinically relevant model of psoriasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing NIK accumulation and p52 processing in Traf2-/- keratinocytes.

claim: The inflammation caused by keratinocyte-specific deletion of Traf2 was driven by the adaptive immune system.
source: This inflammation was driven by TNF, cell death, non-canonical NF-κB and the adaptive immune system, and might therefore represent a clinically relevant model of psoriasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing infiltration of CD4+ T cells and neutrophils.

claim: The Traf2EKO mouse model might represent a clinically relevant model of psoriasis.
source: This inflammation was driven by TNF, cell death, non-canonical NF-κB and the adaptive immune system, and might therefore represent a clinically relevant model of psoriasis.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative conclusion in the abstract based on the observed phenotype.

claim: TRAF2 has essential tissue specific functions that do not overlap with those of Sphk1.
source: TRAF2 therefore has essential tissue specific functions that do not overlap with those of Sphk1.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by comparative data from Traf2 and Sphk1 knockout cells.

claim: TRAF2 was first identified together with TRAF1 as a component of TNF receptor-2 and then TNF receptor-1 (TNFR1) signalling complexes.
source: It was first identified together with TRAF1 as a component of TNF receptor-2 and then TNF receptor-1 (TNFR1) signalling complexes (Rothe et al., 1994; Shu et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: TRAF2 contains a RING domain, several zinc fingers, a TRAF-N, and a conserved TRAF-C domain.
source: TRAF2, like most other TRAFs, contains a RING domain, several zinc fingers, a TRAF-N, and a conserved TRAF-C domain which is responsible for oligomerisation and receptor binding through its MATH region (Takeuchi et al., 1996; Uren and Vaux, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The TRAF-C domain is responsible for oligomerisation and receptor binding through its MATH region.
source: TRAF2, like most other TRAFs, contains a RING domain, several zinc fingers, a TRAF-N, and a conserved TRAF-C domain which is responsible for oligomerisation and receptor binding through its MATH region (Takeuchi et al., 1996; Uren and Vaux, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: RING domains are nearly always associated with ubiquitin E3 ligase activity.
source: RING domains are nearly always associated with ubiquitin E3 ligase activity (Shi and Kehrl, 2003) and TRAF2 can promote ubiquitylation of RIPK1 in TNFR1 signalling complexes (TNFR1-SC) (Wertz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: TRAF2 can promote ubiquitylation of RIPK1 in TNFR1 signalling complexes (TNFR1-SC).
source: RING domains are nearly always associated with ubiquitin E3 ligase activity (Shi and Kehrl, 2003) and TRAF2 can promote ubiquitylation of RIPK1 in TNFR1 signalling complexes (TNFR1-SC) (Wertz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: TRAF2 recruits E3 ligases such as cIAPs to TNFR1-SC.
source: However TRAF2 recruits E3 ligases such as cIAPs to TNFR1-SC and these have also been shown to be able to ubiquitylate RIPK1 and regulate TNF signalling (Dynek et al., 2010; Mahoney et al., 2008; Varfolomeev et al., 2008; Vince et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: cIAPs have been shown to be able to ubiquitylate RIPK1 and regulate TNF signalling.
source: However TRAF2 recruits E3 ligases such as cIAPs to TNFR1-SC and these have also been shown to be able to ubiquitylate RIPK1 and regulate TNF signalling (Dynek et al., 2010; Mahoney et al., 2008; Varfolomeev et al., 2008; Vince et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Activation of JNK and NF-κB by TNF is reduced in cells from Traf2-/- mice.
source: Activation of JNK and NF-κB by TNF is reduced in cells from Traf2-/- mice while only JNK signalling was affected in lymphocytes from transgenic mice that express a dominant negative (DN) form of TRAF2 that lacks the RING domain (Lee et al., 1997; Yeh et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Only JNK signalling was affected in lymphocytes from transgenic mice that express a dominant negative (DN) form of TRAF2 that lacks the RING domain.
source: Activation of JNK and NF-κB by TNF is reduced in cells from Traf2-/- mice while only JNK signalling was affected in lymphocytes from transgenic mice that express a dominant negative (DN) form of TRAF2 that lacks the RING domain (Lee et al., 1997; Yeh et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Traf2-/-Traf5-/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) have a pronounced defect in activation of NF-κB by TNF.
source: Traf2-/-Traf5-/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) have a pronounced defect in activation of NF-κB by TNF, suggesting that absence of TRAF2 can be compensated by TRAF5 (Tada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Absence of TRAF2 can be compensated by TRAF5.
source: Traf2-/-Traf5-/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) have a pronounced defect in activation of NF-κB by TNF, suggesting that absence of TRAF2 can be compensated by TRAF5 (Tada et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from cited work.

claim: Activation of NF-κB was restored in Traf2-/-Traf5-/- cells by re-expression of wild type TRAF2.
source: Although activation of NF-κB was restored in Traf2-/-Traf5-/- cells by re-expression of wild type TRAF2, it was not restored when the cells were reconstituted with TRAF2 point mutants that could not bind cIAPs (Vince et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Activation of NF-κB was not restored in Traf2-/-Traf5-/- cells when the cells were reconstituted with TRAF2 point mutants that could not bind cIAPs.
source: Although activation of NF-κB was restored in Traf2-/-Traf5-/- cells by re-expression of wild type TRAF2, it was not restored when the cells were reconstituted with TRAF2 point mutants that could not bind cIAPs (Vince et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: cIAPs are critical E3 ligases required for TNF-induced canonical NF-κB.
source: These data, together with a wealth of different lines of evidence showing that cIAPs are critical E3 ligases required for TNF-induced canonical NF-κB (Blackwell et al., 2013; Haas et al., 2009; Silke, 2011), support the idea that the main function of TRAF2 in TNF-induced NF-κB is to recruit cIAPs to the TNFR1-SC.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The main function of TRAF2 in TNF-induced NF-κB is to recruit cIAPs to the TNFR1-SC.
source: These data, together with a wealth of different lines of evidence showing that cIAPs are critical E3 ligases required for TNF-induced canonical NF-κB (Blackwell et al., 2013; Haas et al., 2009; Silke, 2011), support the idea that the main function of TRAF2 in TNF-induced NF-κB is to recruit cIAPs to the TNFR1-SC.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an interpretation of cited evidence.

claim: The RING of TRAF2 might play a function in activating JNK and protecting cells from TNF-induced cell death.
source: However, it remains possible that the RING of TRAF2 plays another function, such as in activating JNK and protecting cells from TNF-induced cell death (Vince et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a possibility based on cited work.

claim: TRAF2 can K48-ubiquitylate caspase-8 to set the threshold for TRAIL or Fas induced cell death.
source: Furthermore it has been shown that TRAF2 can K48-ubiquitylate caspase-8 to set the threshold for TRAIL or Fas induced cell death (Gonzalvez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: TRAF2 inhibits non-canonical NF-κB signalling.
source: Moreover, TRAF2 inhibits non-canonical NF-κB signalling (Grech et al., 2004; Zarnegar et al., 2008) and this function requires the RING domain of TRAF2 to induce proteosomal degradation of NIK (Vince et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The function of TRAF2 to inhibit non-canonical NF-κB signalling requires the RING domain of TRAF2 to induce proteosomal degradation of NIK.
source: Moreover, TRAF2 inhibits non-canonical NF-κB signalling (Grech et al., 2004; Zarnegar et al., 2008) and this function requires the RING domain of TRAF2 to induce proteosomal degradation of NIK (Vince et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Structural and in vitro analyses indicate that the RING domain of TRAF2 is unable to bind E2 conjugating enzymes.
source: However, structural and in vitro analyses indicate that, unlike TRAF6, the RING domain of TRAF2 is unable to bind E2 conjugating enzymes (Yin et al., 2009), and is therefore unlikely to have intrinsic E3 ligase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The RING domain of TRAF2 is unlikely to have intrinsic E3 ligase activity.
source: However, structural and in vitro analyses indicate that, unlike TRAF6, the RING domain of TRAF2 is unable to bind E2 conjugating enzymes (Yin et al., 2009), and is therefore unlikely to have intrinsic E3 ligase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from cited structural data.

claim: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is a pleiotropic sphingolipid mediator that regulates proliferation, differentiation, cell trafficking and vascular development.
source: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is a pleiotropic sphingolipid mediator that regulates proliferation, differentiation, cell trafficking and vascular development (Pitson, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: S1P is generated by sphingosine kinase 1 and 2 (SPHK1 and SPHK2).
source: S1P is generated by sphingosine kinase 1 and 2 (SPHK1 and SPHK2) (Kohama et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Extracellular S1P mainly acts by binding to its five G protein-coupled receptors S1P1-5.
source: Extracellular S1P mainly acts by binding to its five G protein-coupled receptors S1P1-5 (Hla and Dannenberg, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Some intracellular roles have been suggested for S1P, including the blocking of the histone deacetylases, HDAC1/2.
source: However, some intracellular roles have been suggested for S1P, including the blocking of the histone deacetylases, HDAC1/2 (Hait et al., 2009) and the induction of apoptosis through interaction with BAK and BAX (Chipuk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Some intracellular roles have been suggested for S1P, including the induction of apoptosis through interaction with BAK and BAX.
source: However, some intracellular roles have been suggested for S1P, including the blocking of the histone deacetylases, HDAC1/2 (Hait et al., 2009) and the induction of apoptosis through interaction with BAK and BAX (Chipuk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: It was suggested that the RING domain of TRAF2 requires S1P as a co-factor for its E3 ligase activity.
source: Recently, it was suggested that the RING domain of TRAF2 requires S1P as a co-factor for its E3 ligase activity (Alvarez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Alvarez and colleagues proposed that SPHK1 but not SPHK2 is activated by TNF and phosphorylates sphingosine to S1P.
source: Alvarez and colleagues proposed that SPHK1 but not SPHK2 is activated by TNF and phosphorylates sphingosine to S1P which in turn binds to the RING domain of TRAF2 and serves as an essential co-factor that was missing in the experiments of Yin et al.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of Alvarez et al.'s proposal.

claim: S1P binds to the RING domain of TRAF2 and serves as an essential co-factor.
source: Alvarez and colleagues proposed that SPHK1 but not SPHK2 is activated by TNF and phosphorylates sphingosine to S1P which in turn binds to the RING domain of TRAF2 and serves as an essential co-factor that was missing in the experiments of Yin et al.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of Alvarez et al.'s proposal.

claim: Alvarez and colleagues observed that in the absence of SPHK1, TNF-induced NF-κB activation was completely abolished.
source: Alvarez and colleagues, observed that in the absence of SPHK1, TNF-induced NF-κB activation was completely abolished.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of Alvarez et al.'s findings.

claim: Neither TRAF2 nor SPHK1 are required for TNF mediated canonical NF-κB and MAPK signalling in macrophages.
source: Surprisingly, we found that neither TRAF2 nor SPHK1 are required for TNF mediated canonical NF-κB and MAPK signalling in macrophages.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1.

claim: MEFs, murine dermal fibroblasts (MDFs) and keratinocytes required TRAF2 but not SPHK1 for full strength TNF signalling.
source: However, MEFs, murine dermal fibroblasts (MDFs) and keratinocytes required TRAF2 but not SPHK1 for full strength TNF signalling.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 2.

claim: Absence of TRAF2 caused a delay in TNF-induced activation of NF-κB and MAPK in MEFs, MDFs and keratinocytes.
source: In these cell types, absence of TRAF2 caused a delay in TNF-induced activation of NF-κB and MAPK, and sensitivity to killing by TNF was increased.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 2.

claim: Absence of TRAF2 increased sensitivity to killing by TNF in MEFs, MDFs and keratinocytes.
source: In these cell types, absence of TRAF2 caused a delay in TNF-induced activation of NF-κB and MAPK, and sensitivity to killing by TNF was increased.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by cell death assay data in Figure 2.

claim: Absence of TRAF2 in keratinocytes in vivo resulted in psoriasis-like epidermal hyperplasia and skin inflammation.
source: Absence of TRAF2 in keratinocytes in vivo resulted in psoriasis-like epidermal hyperplasia and skin inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by histological images in Figure 4.

claim: The onset of inflammation in Traf2EKO mice was only delayed, and not prevented by deletion of TNF.
source: Unlike TNF-dependent genetic inflammatory skin conditions, such as IKK2 epidermal knock-out (Pasparakis et al., 2002) and the cpdm mutant (Gerlach et al., 2011), the onset of inflammation was only delayed, and not prevented by deletion of TNF.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by survival data and images in Figure 4.

claim: The early TNF-dependent inflammation in Traf2EKO mice is caused by excessive apoptotic but not necroptotic cell death.
source: This early TNF-dependent inflammation is caused by excessive apoptotic but not necroptotic cell death and could be prevented by deletion of Casp8.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 5 showing rescue by Casp8 deletion but not Mlkl deletion.

claim: The early TNF-dependent inflammation in Traf2EKO mice could be prevented by deletion of Casp8.
source: This early TNF-dependent inflammation is caused by excessive apoptotic but not necroptotic cell death and could be prevented by deletion of Casp8.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Constitutive activation of NIK and non-canonical NF-κB was observed in Traf2-/- keratinocytes.
source: We observed constitutive activation of NIK and non-canonical NF-κB in Traf2-/- keratinocytes which caused production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 8.

claim: Constitutive activation of NIK and non-canonical NF-κB in Traf2-/- keratinocytes caused production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
source: We observed constitutive activation of NIK and non-canonical NF-κB in Traf2-/- keratinocytes which caused production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data in Figure 8.

claim: The inflammatory phenotype in Traf2EKO mice could be reversed by simultaneously deleting both Tnf and Nfkb2 genes.
source: We were able to reverse this inflammatory phenotype by simultaneously deleting both Tnf and Nfkb2 genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 10.

claim: TNF-dependent cell death, but not non-canonical NF-κB, is a driver of the early inflammation in Traf2EKO mice.
source: These data show that TNF-dependent cell death, but not non-canonical NF-κB, is a driver of the early inflammation in Traf2EKO mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the genetic rescue experiments.

claim: Constitutive activation of non-canonical NF-κB in Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice might be responsible for the later onset skin disease.
source: Constitutive activation of non-canonical NF-κB in Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice might, however, be responsible for the later onset skin disease that developed in these Tnf-deficient mice (Figure 11).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative interpretation.

claim: TNF stimulation of wild type BMDMs caused degradation of IκBα and phosphorylation of JNK and ERK within 15 min.
source: TNF stimulation of wild type BMDMs caused degradation of IκBα and phosphorylation of JNK and ERK within 15 min (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In Traf2LC and Sphk1 deficient BMDMs, the kinetics of IκBα degradation and phosphorylation of JNK and ERK induced by TNF were the same as in wild-type BMDMs.
source: In Traf2LC and Sphk1 deficient BMDMs, the kinetics of IκBα degradation and phosphorylation of JNK and ERK induced by TNF were the same as in wild-type BMDMs (Figure 1A and 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: TNF was not cytotoxic to either wild-type or Traf2-/- macrophages.
source: Taking into account the slightly higher background death of Traf2-/- BMDMs compared with wild type BMDMs, TNF was not cytotoxic to either wild-type or Traf2-/- macrophages (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Wild-type macrophages were resistant to killing by low-dose SM, but Traf2LC BMDMs were very sensitive.
source: As previously reported, wild-type macrophages were resistant to killing by low-dose SM, but Traf2LC BMDMs were very sensitive (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the amount of TNF secreted by wild type or Traf2LC macrophages at 20 hr after TNF stimulation.
source: Increased TNF secretion was undetectable earlier than 20 hr after TNF stimulation and there was no significant difference in the amount of TNF secreted by wild type or Traf2LC macrophages at this time point (Figure 1D; upper panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After 4 hr of treatment with SM, very large amounts of TNF could be detected in both the wild-type and Traf2LC macrophages.
source: In contrast, after 4 hr of treatment with SM, very large amounts of TNF could be detected in both the wild-type and Traf2LC macrophages (Figure 1D; lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After 8 hr the amount of TNF secreted by the Traf2LC macrophages was less than that made by the wild-type macrophages.
source: Although initially similar amounts of TNF were produced, after 8 hr the amount of TNF secreted by the Traf2LC macrophages was less than that made by the wild-type macrophages (Figure 1D; lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The reduced TNF secretion by Traf2LC macrophages after 8 hr is probably due to SM-induced death of Traf2LC but not wild-type BMDMs.
source: This is probably due to SM-induced death of Traf2LC but not wild-type BMDMs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the cell death data in Figure 1C.

claim: Loss of TRAF2 in MEFs caused a delay in, but did not abolish, TNF-induced NF-κB activation and JNK phosphorylation.
source: Consistent with earlier reports (Tada et al., 2001; Vince et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010), loss of TRAF2 in MEFs caused a delay in, but did not abolish, TNF-induced NF-κB activation and JNK phosphorylation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Loss of TRAF2 in MDFs caused a delay in both NF-κB and MAPK signalling activation.
source: Similarly, loss of TRAF2 in MDFs caused a delay in both NF-κB and MAPK signalling activation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No delay in TNF signalling was observed in Sphk1 knock-out MEFs and MDFs.
source: However, no such delay was observed in Sphk1 knock-out cells (Figure 2A and 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Traf2 knock-out MEFs and MDFs were sensitive to TNF-induced cell death.
source: Consistent with earlier findings (Vince et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010), Traf2 knock-out MEFs and MDFs were sensitive to TNF-induced cell death; however, wild-type and Sphk1-/- cells remained resistant (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Wild-type and Sphk1-/- MEFs and MDFs remained resistant to TNF-induced cell death.
source: Consistent with earlier findings (Vince et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010), Traf2 knock-out MEFs and MDFs were sensitive to TNF-induced cell death; however, wild-type and Sphk1-/- cells remained resistant (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The sensitivity to TNF-induced cell death correlated with caspase-8 and -3 cleavage in Traf2-/- fibroblasts.
source: The sensitivity to TNF-induced cell death correlated with caspase-8 and -3 cleavage in Traf2-/- fibroblasts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TNF signalling was delayed and weakened in Traf2-deficient keratinocytes.
source: Primary keratinocytes isolated from wild-type, Traf2EKO and Sphk1-/- mice were tested and, similarly to MEFs and MDFs, TNF signalling was delayed and weakened in Traf2-deficient (Figure 2D), but not Sphk1-deficient keratinocytes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TNF signalling was not delayed or weakened in Sphk1-deficient keratinocytes.
source: Primary keratinocytes isolated from wild-type, Traf2EKO and Sphk1-/- mice were tested and, similarly to MEFs and MDFs, TNF signalling was delayed and weakened in Traf2-deficient (Figure 2D), but not Sphk1-deficient keratinocytes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Traf2-/-, but not Sphk1-/-, keratinocytes were sensitive to TNF-induced death.
source: Traf2-/-, but not Sphk1-/-, keratinocytes were also sensitive to TNF-induced death (Figure 2F), and this was associated with a rapid reduction in cFLIPL levels and caspase-8 cleavage (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MTS assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TNF-induced death of Traf2-/- keratinocytes was associated with a rapid reduction in cFLIPL levels and caspase-8 cleavage.
source: Traf2-/-, but not Sphk1-/-, keratinocytes were also sensitive to TNF-induced death (Figure 2F), and this was associated with a rapid reduction in cFLIPL levels and caspase-8 cleavage (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment with the pan-caspase inhibitor Q-VD-OPh (QVD) reduced TNF-induced death of Traf2-/- keratinocytes by about half.
source: Treatment with the pan-caspase inhibitor Q-VD-OPh (QVD) reduced TNF-induced death of Traf2-/- cells by about half (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MTS assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The combination of QVD and Nec completely blocked TNF-induced cell death in Traf2-/- keratinocytes.
source: However, the combination of QVD and Nec completely blocked TNF-induced cell death in Traf2-/- keratinocytes (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MTS assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Within 5 to 15 min of TNF stimulation RIPK1 became strongly ubiquitylated in both wild-type and Sphk1-/- MDFs.
source: Within 5 to 15 min of TNF stimulation RIPK1 became strongly ubiquitylated in both wild-type and Sphk1-/- MDFs, and this decreased over 60 min (Figure 3A and 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TUBE IP data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: RIPK1 ubiquitylation decreased over 60 min in wild-type and Sphk1-/- MDFs.
source: Within 5 to 15 min of TNF stimulation RIPK1 became strongly ubiquitylated in both wild-type and Sphk1-/- MDFs, and this decreased over 60 min (Figure 3A and 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TUBE IP data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: In Traf2-/- cells, RIPK1 ubiquitylation was not observed at early time points (5 or 15 min), but occurred after 60 min with a different pattern.
source: In Traf2-/- cells, this ubiquitylation was not observed at early time points (5 or 15 min), but occurred after 60 min with a different pattern (Figure 3A and 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TUBE IP data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The delayed ubiquitylation of RIPK1 in Traf2-/- cells correlated with the delayed NF-κB activation observed in Traf2-/- cells.
source: This delayed ubiquitylation correlated with the delayed NF-κB activation observed in Traf2-/- cells (Figure 2A,B and 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a correlation between two observed phenomena.

claim: cIAP1 and phospho-ERK migrated as high molecular weight species, suggestive of ubiquitylation, within 15 min of TNF stimulation in wild type and Sphk1-/-.
source: cIAP1 and phospho-ERK migrated as high molecular weight species, suggestive of ubiquitylation, within 15 min of TNF stimulation in wild type and Sphk1-/-, but this ubiquitylation was delayed in Traf2-/- MDFs (Figure 3A and 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TUBE IP data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Ubiquitylation of cIAP1 and phospho-ERK was delayed in Traf2-/- MDFs.
source: cIAP1 and phospho-ERK migrated as high molecular weight species, suggestive of ubiquitylation, within 15 min of TNF stimulation in wild type and Sphk1-/-, but this ubiquitylation was delayed in Traf2-/- MDFs (Figure 3A and 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TUBE IP data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Cleaved caspase-8 appeared in Traf2-/- MDFs after 1 hr TNF stimulation.
source: Consistent with the previous results, cleaved caspase-8 appeared in Traf2-/- MDFs after 1 hr TNF stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Traf2EKO mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratios.
source: Traf2EKO mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratios but developed an inflamed skin phenotype from 6 weeks of age.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from breeding experiments.

claim: Traf2EKO mice developed an inflamed skin phenotype from 6 weeks of age.
source: Traf2EKO mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratios but developed an inflamed skin phenotype from 6 weeks of age.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figure 4.

claim: The skin phenotype in Traf2EKO mice became worse over time and the mice were sacrificed usually before 15 weeks of age.
source: This phenotype became worse over time and the mice were sacrificed usually before 15 weeks of age (Figure 4A and 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by survival data in Figure 4F.

claim: The epidermal layer in a normal mouse is usually composed of 2–3 layers of keratinocytes.
source: The epidermal layer in a normal mouse is usually composed of 2–3 layers of keratinocytes (Gudjonsson et al., 2007); however, histological skin sections from Traf2EKO mice revealed a grossly thickened epidermis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Histological skin sections from Traf2EKO mice revealed a grossly thickened epidermis.
source: The epidermal layer in a normal mouse is usually composed of 2–3 layers of keratinocytes (Gudjonsson et al., 2007); however, histological skin sections from Traf2EKO mice revealed a grossly thickened epidermis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by histological images in Figure 4B.

claim: Normally, the epidermis expresses keratin-14, but keratin-6 expression is confined to hair follicles or hyper-proliferative keratinocytes.
source: Normally, the epidermis expresses keratin-14, but keratin-6 expression is confined to hair follicles or hyper-proliferative keratinocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the results as background knowledge.

claim: The Traf2EKO epidermis was highlighted by widespread expression of both keratin-14 and keratin-6.
source: The Traf2EKO epidermis was highlighted by widespread expression of both of these markers (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 4B.

claim: Excessive leukocyte infiltration was detected in the inflamed area of Traf2EKO by immunostaining of CD45.
source: Excessive leukocyte infiltration and apoptotic death were also detected in the inflamed area of Traf2EKO by immunostaining of CD45 (leukocyte common antigen) and cleaved caspase-3 (CC3), respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figure 4B.

claim: Apoptotic death was detected in the inflamed area of Traf2EKO by immunostaining of cleaved caspase-3 (CC3).
source: Excessive leukocyte infiltration and apoptotic death were also detected in the inflamed area of Traf2EKO by immunostaining of CD45 (leukocyte common antigen) and cleaved caspase-3 (CC3), respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figure 4B.

claim: No significant infiltration of mast cells into the inflamed area of Traf2EKO mice was detected by toluidine blue staining.
source: We did not detect any significant infiltration of mast cells into the inflamed area of Traf2EKO mice by toluidine blue staining (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by toluidine blue staining images in Figure 4B.

claim: Traf2-/- keratinocytes spontaneously secrete TNF in culture.
source: Based on the presence of apoptotic cells in the epidermal layer of Traf2EKO mice (Figure 4B), spontaneous secretion of TNF by Traf2-/- keratinocytes in culture (Figure 4C) and the disrupted TNF signalling in Traf2-/- keratinocytes (Figure 2D), we hypothesised that depletion of TNF would also prevent the inflammation in the skin of Traf2EKO mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice did not develop epidermal hyperplasia and skin inflammation at the same time as Traf2EKO mice.
source: Therefore, Traf2EKO mice were crossed to Tnf-/- mice. Consistent with our hypothesis, Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice did not develop epidermal hyperplasia and skin inflammation at the same time as Traf2EKO mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figure 4D.

claim: At ~20 weeks after birth (10 weeks later than Traf2EKO), the skin of most of the Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice started to become inflamed.
source: However, at ~20 weeks after birth (10 weeks later than Traf2EKO), the skin of most of the Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice started to become inflamed.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images and survival data in Figure 4.

claim: Lesions in Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice became severe by 30 weeks, and these necessitated sacrifice of the affected animals.
source: Lesions became severe by 30 weeks, and these necessitated sacrifice of the affected animals (Figure 4D and 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images and survival data in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: Leukocyte infiltration into the dermis of 10-week-old Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice was reduced when compared to age-matched Traf2EKO mice.
source: Histological analysis revealed that leukocyte infiltration into the dermis of 10-week-old Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice was also reduced when compared to age-matched Traf2EKO mice, but increased by 23 weeks (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figure 4E.

claim: Leukocyte infiltration into the dermis of Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice increased by 23 weeks.
source: Histological analysis revealed that leukocyte infiltration into the dermis of 10-week-old Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice was also reduced when compared to age-matched Traf2EKO mice, but increased by 23 weeks (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figure 4E.

claim: There was no evidence for apoptotic, cleaved caspase 3 (CC3)-positive cells in the skin of Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice at any age.
source: There was no evidence for apoptotic, cleaved caspase 3 (CC3)-positive cells in the skin of Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice at any age, suggesting that cell death is induced by TNF in the Traf2-/- mice (Figure 4B) and that increased proliferation can be genetically separated from apoptotic cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunohistochemistry images in Figure 4E.

claim: Cell death is induced by TNF in the Traf2-/- mice.
source: There was no evidence for apoptotic, cleaved caspase 3 (CC3)-positive cells in the skin of Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice at any age, suggesting that cell death is induced by TNF in the Traf2-/- mice (Figure 4B) and that increased proliferation can be genetically separated from apoptotic cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the absence of apoptotic cells in Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice.

claim: Increased proliferation can be genetically separated from apoptotic cell death in Traf2EKO mice.
source: There was no evidence for apoptotic, cleaved caspase 3 (CC3)-positive cells in the skin of Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice at any age, suggesting that cell death is induced by TNF in the Traf2-/- mice (Figure 4B) and that increased proliferation can be genetically separated from apoptotic cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the phenotype of Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice.

claim: Depletion of MLKL did not prevent or alter the onset of the skin inflammation in Traf2EKO mice.
source: However, depletion of MLKL, an essential necroptosis effector (Murphy et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2012), did not prevent or alter the onset of the skin inflammation in Traf2EKO mice (Figure 5A and 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Deficiency of both MLKL and caspase-8 rescued the early skin inflammation in Traf2EKO.
source: Deficiency of both MLKL and caspase-8 did, however, rescue the early skin inflammation in Traf2EKO (Figure 5A and 5B) but the mice could not be aged further because Mlkl-/-Casp8-/- mice develop lymphadenopathy before 15 weeks of age (Alvarez-Diaz et al., personal communication, October 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Oligomerisation of MLKL in the membrane fraction did not occur following 5 hr of TNF stimulation in Traf2-/- keratinocytes.
source: Oligomerisation of MLKL in the membrane fraction is a marker for execution of necroptosis (Hildebrand et al., 2014) and did not occur following 5 hr of TNF stimulation, but was only seen when caspases were inhibited by Q-VD-OPh (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Blue Native PAGE data in Figure 5C.

claim: Oligomerisation of MLKL was only seen when caspases were inhibited by Q-VD-OPh in Traf2-/- keratinocytes.
source: Oligomerisation of MLKL in the membrane fraction is a marker for execution of necroptosis (Hildebrand et al., 2014) and did not occur following 5 hr of TNF stimulation, but was only seen when caspases were inhibited by Q-VD-OPh (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Blue Native PAGE data in Figure 5C.

claim: Oligomerisation of MLKL induced by TNF and Q-VD-OPh treatment was blocked by Necrostatin in Traf2-/- keratinocytes.
source: As expected, however, oligomerisation of MLKL induced by TNF and Q-VD-OPh treatment was blocked by Necrostatin (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Blue Native PAGE data in Figure 5C.

claim: The skin from Traf2EKO and Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice had higher numbers of CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils in the epidermal and dermal layers compared to wild-type skin.
source: The skin from Traf2EKO and Traf2EKOTnf-/- mice had higher numbers of CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils in the epidermal and dermal layers compared to wild-type skin (Figure 6A,B,C and 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 6A-D.

claim: CD4+ T cells were abundant in the inflamed skin of Traf2EKO and Traf2EKOTnf-/-.
source: CD4+ T cells were also abundant in the inflamed skin of Traf2EKO and Traf2EKOTnf-/- (Figure 6E and 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: IFNγ producing CD4+ T cells were significantly more abundant in the skin of Traf2EKOTnf-/- than Traf2EKO.
source: Surprisingly, IFNγ producing CD4+ T cells were significantly more abundant in the skin of Traf2EKOTnf-/- than Traf2EKO (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6G.

claim: Both wild type and Ifng-/- chimeras developed skin inflammation to the same extent.
source: However, both wild type and Ifng-/- chimeras developed skin inflammation to the same extent, indicating that hematopoietic cell-derived IFNγ is not a major contributor to the psoriasis-like skin inflammation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figure 7.

claim: Hematopoietic cell-derived IFNγ is not a major contributor to the psoriasis-like skin inflammation in Traf2EKO mice.
source: However, both wild type and Ifng-/- chimeras developed skin inflammation to the same extent, indicating that hematopoietic cell-derived IFNγ is not a major contributor to the psoriasis-like skin inflammation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the bone marrow chimera experiment.

claim: NIK was readily detectable in Traf2-/- but not wild-type keratinocytes.
source: Consistent with non-canonical NF-κB activation, NIK was readily detectable in Traf2-/- but not wild-type keratinocytes and there were higher levels of p52 in these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 8A.

claim: There were higher levels of p52 in Traf2-/- keratinocytes compared to wild-type.
source: Consistent with non-canonical NF-κB activation, NIK was readily detectable in Traf2-/- but not wild-type keratinocytes and there were higher levels of p52 in these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 8A.

claim: Activation of non-canonical NF-κB in Traf2-/- keratinocytes was likely independent of TNF.
source: This activation of non-canonical NF-κB was likely independent of TNF because stimulation of these cells for 2 hr with TNF did not change the level of NIK or p52 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the Western blot data in Figure 8A.

claim: No difference was observed in the proliferation of Traf2-/- versus wild-type keratinocytes on a Tnf-/- background.
source: However, no difference was observed in the proliferation of Traf2-/- versus wild-type keratinocytes (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MTS assay data in Figure 8B.

claim: Traf2-/- keratinocytes were sensitive to TNF and gave a very low MTS value.
source: As expected, Traf2-/- keratinocytes were sensitive to TNF and gave a very low MTS value, while Traf2+/- keratinocytes, generated from littermate controls, were resistant to TNF-induced death (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MTS assay data in Figure 8B.

claim: Traf2+/- keratinocytes were resistant to TNF-induced death.
source: As expected, Traf2-/- keratinocytes were sensitive to TNF and gave a very low MTS value, while Traf2+/- keratinocytes, generated from littermate controls, were resistant to TNF-induced death (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MTS assay data in Figure 8B.

claim: Loss of TRAF2 did not affect IL-17 signalling in Traf2-/- keratinocytes, as assessed by IκBα degradation and phosphorylation of p65 and p38.
source: However, loss of TRAF2 did not affect IL-17 signalling in Traf2-/- keratinocytes, as assessed by IκBα degradation and phosphorylation of p65 and p38 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data in Figure 8C.

claim: Stimulation of keratinocytes by IL-17 did not induce proliferation of keratinocytes either in wild-type or Traf2-/- keratinocytes in vitro.
source: Moreover, stimulation of keratinocytes by IL-17 did not induce proliferation of keratinocytes either in wild-type or Traf2-/- keratinocytes in vitro (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MTS assay data in Figure 8D.

claim: Out of more than 600 inflammatory genes analysed, about 300 genes were constitutively expressed in the keratinocytes under serum-free conditions.
source: Out of more than 600 inflammatory genes analysed, about 300 genes were constitutively expressed in the keratinocytes under these conditions (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR array data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The signature of inflammatory genes expression was changed in Traf2-/-Tnf-/- compared to Traf2+/-Tnf-/- keratinocytes.
source: The signature of inflammatory genes expression was changed in Traf2-/-Tnf-/- compared to Traf2+/-Tnf-/- keratinocytes (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR array data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Many inflammatory genes, such as Csf1 (M-CSF), IL-23, TNFSF9 (4-1BBL), Cr1l and Cxcl16, were highly elevated in Traf2-/-Tnf-/- keratinocytes.
source: Many inflammatory genes, such as Csf1 (M-CSF), IL-23, TNFSF9 (4-1BBL), Cr1l and Cxcl16, were highly elevated in Traf2-/-Tnf-/- keratinocytes (an Excel list and zoom-able heat map of 338 expressed genes are available as Figure 8—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR array data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Deletion of one allele of NIK prevents lethality of Traf2 knock-out.
source: Deletion of one allele of NIK prevents lethality of Traf2 knock-out (Lin et al., 2011; Vallabhapurapu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: Deficiency in Map3k14 or Nfkb2 did not prevent the psoriasis-like skin disease in Traf2EKO mice.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, deficiency in Map3k14 or Nfkb2 did not prevent the psoriasis-like skin disease in Traf2EKO mice (Figure 9 and 10).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/+ and Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly mice developed skin inflammation.
source: Not only did Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/+ and Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly mice develop skin inflammation, the onset of disease in Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly mice was earlier than in Traf2EKO or Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/+ mice (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images and survival data in Figure 9.

claim: The onset of disease in Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly mice was earlier than in Traf2EKO or Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/+ mice.
source: Not only did Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/+ and Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly mice develop skin inflammation, the onset of disease in Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly mice was earlier than in Traf2EKO or Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/+ mice (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by survival data in Figure 9.

claim: Traf2EKONfkb2-/- mice developed epidermal hyperplasia and skin inflammation in the same time frame as Traf2EKO animals.
source: Traf2EKONfkb2-/- mice developed epidermal hyperplasia and skin inflammation in the same time frame as Traf2EKO animals (Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figure 10.

claim: The location of skin disease in both Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly and Traf2EKONfkb2-/- was different to that in Traf2EKO animals.
source: Furthermore, the location of skin disease in both Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly and Traf2EKONfkb2-/- was different to that in Traf2EKO animals (Figures 9A and 10C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figures 9A and 10C.

claim: Loss of Traf2 usually caused lesions in the submental and forehead area.
source: Loss of Traf2 usually caused lesions in the submental and forehead area, while lesions in Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly and Traf2EKONfkb2-/- mice appeared around the legs and sometimes spread over the whole ventral area (Figures 9A, 10A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figures 9A and 10A,C.

claim: Lesions in Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly and Traf2EKONfkb2-/- mice appeared around the legs and sometimes spread over the whole ventral area.
source: Loss of Traf2 usually caused lesions in the submental and forehead area, while lesions in Traf2EKOMap3k14aly/aly and Traf2EKONfkb2-/- mice appeared around the legs and sometimes spread over the whole ventral area (Figures 9A, 10A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figures 9A and 10A,C.

claim: Depletion of both TNF and NF-κB2 completely prevent the psoriasis-like inflammation in the Traf2EKO mice.
source: However, depletion of both TNF and NF-κB2 completely prevent the psoriasis-like inflammation in the Traf2EKO mice (Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images and survival data in Figure 10.

claim: Three out of thirteen of the Traf2EKOTnf-/-Nfkb2-/- mice developed skin lesions at an early age around the mouth and anus.
source: Three out of thirteen of the Traf2EKOTnf-/-Nfkb2-/- mice developed skin lesions at an early age around the mouth and anus (Figure 10C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by images in Figure 10C,D.

claim: The early skin lesions in Traf2EKOTnf-/-Nfkb2-/- mice are likely due to the susceptibility of NFκB2 deficient mice to opportunistic infections.
source: This is likely to be due to the susceptibility of NFκB2 deficient mice to opportunistic infections because both Tnf-/-Nfkb2-/- and Traf2EKO/EKONfkb2-/- mice also succumbed to such infections (Figure 10C) and (Shinkura et al., 1996; Yin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference supported by cited literature.

claim: Most of the Traf2EKOTnf-/-Nfkb2-/- mice were healthy up to 36 weeks of age without showing any sign of inflammation.
source: However, most of the Traf2EKOTnf-/-Nfkb2-/- mice were healthy up to 36 weeks of age without showing any sign of inflammation (Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by survival data in Figure 10.

claim: Inhibition of non-canonical NF-κB signalling might be beneficial in chronic inflammatory disease together with TNF inhibitors.
source: Thus, our results suggest that inhibition of non-canonical NF-κB signalling might be beneficial in chronic inflammatory disease together with TNF inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative conclusion based on the results.

claim: The levels of TWEAK and its receptor Fn-14 are elevated in human psoriatic lesions.
source: This observation might be relevant to human psoriasis because it has been reported that the levels of TWEAK and its receptor Fn-14 are elevated in human psoriatic lesions (Cheng et al., 2015), and it is well established that TWEAK/Fn14 signalling induces degradation of TRAF2 and activation of non-canonical NF-κB signalling (Saitoh et al., 2003; Vince et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: TWEAK/Fn14 signalling induces degradation of TRAF2 and activation of non-canonical NF-κB signalling.
source: This observation might be relevant to human psoriasis because it has been reported that the levels of TWEAK and its receptor Fn-14 are elevated in human psoriatic lesions (Cheng et al., 2015), and it is well established that TWEAK/Fn14 signalling induces degradation of TRAF2 and activation of non-canonical NF-κB signalling (Saitoh et al., 2003; Vince et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.
